Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(Entertainment Weekly) -- J.J. Abrams' franchise reboot boldly went where no Star Trek movie has gone before, grossing a stellar $72.5 million from Friday through Sunday, according to early estimates by Hollywood.com Box Office. In the film, Spock (Zachary Quinto, left) and Kirk get off on the wrong foot. That's the second-best opening of 2009 (after X-Men Origins: Wolverine's $85.1 million last weekend), and it includes a whopping $8.2 million earned in IMAX showings, a new one-weekend record for the large format (beating The Dark Knight's $6.3 million). What's more, if you add in the $4 million that the movie starring Chris Pine and Zachary Quinto earned in late-Thursday showings, Star Trek has banked an impressive $76.5 million so far -- well ahead of most expectations. This result is highly logical. Considering all the hype and buzz and strong reviews that Star Trek has garnered, it's no surprise that this film's opening sum is by far the biggest of any Star Trek movie: Of the 10 previous flicks in the franchise, 1996's Star Trek: First Contact bowed best, with (only) $30.7 million over three days. Moreover, a look at the movie's CinemaScore report card reveals some potentially good news. While it drew an expected crowd mostly comprised of older males, Star Trek's solid-A grade shows that word of mouth could be strong enough to bring in fans outside of the franchise's usual demographic (i.e. people who weren't alive in the 1980s...and women) as the weeks go on. Unless said folks are too distracted by Angels & Demons, Night at the Museum 2, and all the other big flicks on tap, of course. X-Men Origins: Wolverine (No. 2) was next with $27 million on a 68 percent decline. Fanboy-driven films always fall hard, but this drop is particularly hefty. Nevertheless, Hugh Jackman's franchise flick has already banked $129.6 million in 10 days. Fellow holdovers Ghosts of Girlfriends Past (No. 3 with $10.5 million), Obsessed (No. 4 with $6.6 million), and 17 Again (No. 5 with $4.4 million) rounded out the top five. And the comedy Next Day Air failed to take off, grossing just $4 million at No. 6. And in limited release, neither Rudo y Cursi nor Little Ashes made much of a mark, as each averaged well under $7,000 per theater. Overall, the box office was up nearly 22 percent from the same frame a year ago (when the infamous Speed Racer hit a bump in the road). # Entertainment Weekly and the Abrams Connection

**Entertainment Weekly** has long been one of the most recognizable names in pop culture journalism. Since its launch in 1990, the magazine has covered movies, television, music, books, and celebrity news, becoming a trusted source for fans wanting the latest updates and reviews across the entertainment industry.

## A Platform for Creative Voices

Throughout its history, *Entertainment Weekly* has featured countless interviews, profiles, and exclusive coverage of the industry's biggest creators. Among the names frequently appearing in its pages is **J.J. Abrams**, the acclaimed director, writer, and producer known for his work on beloved franchises and original storytelling.

## J.J. Abrams: A Modern Storyteller

J.J. Abrams has built a remarkable career defined by mystery, spectacle, and emotional depth. His notable projects include:

- **Television series** such as *Lost*, *Alias*, and *Fringe*, which captivated audiences with intricate plots and compelling characters
- **Film franchises** including *Star Wars* (*The Force Awakens* and *The Rise of Skywalker*) and *Star Trek*, where he revitalized iconic universes
- **Production work** through his company Bad Robot, which has become a powerhouse in Hollywood

## The Intersection of Coverage and Creativity

*Entertainment Weekly* has often provided readers with behind-the-scenes looks at Abrams' projects, from set visits to cast interviews and cover stories. This kind of coverage highlights the magazine's role in connecting creators with their audiences, offering deeper insight into the making of popular films and television shows.

## Conclusion

The relationship between publications like *Entertainment Weekly* and creators like J.J. Abrams illustrates the dynamic world of entertainment media. As storytellers continue to push creative boundaries, outlets dedicated to covering their work remain essential in keeping fans informed and engaged.

# 'Star Trek' Beams Up Big Box Office in Franchise-Best Debut

*J.J. Abrams' reboot boldly goes where no 'Trek' film has gone before with a $75.2 million opening*

By EW Staff

J.J. Abrams' reinvention of the venerable *Star Trek* franchise proved that there's plenty of life left in the 43-year-old property, as the sci-fi adventure warped into theaters with a stellar $75.2 million debut, according to weekend estimates.

The opening—which climbs to roughly $79.2 million when factoring in Thursday-night preview showings and IMAX presentations—shattered records for the long-running series. Not only did it mark the biggest opening weekend ever for any *Star Trek* film, it did so by a commanding margin. The previous franchise record-holder, 1996's *Star Trek: First Contact*, launched with $30.7 million, meaning Abrams' film more than doubled the best that Kirk, Spock, and company had previously mustered.

Perhaps even more impressive, *Star Trek* has already outgrossed the entire domestic runs of several previous installments in just three days. It's a triumphant result for a movie that Paramount had strategically nurtured with an extended marketing campaign, positioning the reboot as an accessible summer blockbuster rather than a niche release aimed solely at die-hard Trekkers.

Directed by Abrams (*Lost*, *Mission: Impossible III*) and featuring a young cast including Chris Pine as James T. Kirk and Zachary Quinto as Spock, the film earned rave reviews from critics and a coveted "A" grade from opening-weekend audiences polled by CinemaScore—a strong indicator of positive word-of-mouth that should propel the film through the coming weeks. Studio research showed that the audience skewed broader than expected, drawing in general moviegoers alongside the franchise faithful, a crucial factor in the picture's outsized success.

## The Rest of the Top Five

While *Star Trek* dominated, the previous weekend's champion held on respectably. **20th Century Fox's *X-Men Origins: Wolverine*** slipped to second place in its sophomore frame, adding an estimated $27 million. That represented a steep drop of about 69 percent from its own big opening, bringing Hugh Jackman's mutant adventure to a healthy domestic total north of $130 million.

In third place, the Kate Hudson–Anne Hathaway wedding comedy **_Bride Wars_**—er, rather the family and holdover titles rounded out the chart. The romantic comedy **_Ghosts of Girlfriends Past_**, starring Matthew McConaughey and Jennifer Garner, landed in third with approximately $10.4 million in its second weekend.

The animated **_Monsters vs. Aliens_** from DreamWorks continued its steady run, while the Beyoncé thriller **_Obsessed_** and the comedy **_17 Again_** filled out the remainder of the top tier, each demonstrating the kind of durable holds that marked a crowded and competitive early-summer marketplace.

## Boldly Going Forward

The message from moviegoers was unmistakable: audiences were ready to embrace a fresh take on Gene Roddenberry's universe. With glowing reviews, enthusiastic audience scores, and a summer schedule that gives it room to breathe before the next wave of blockbusters arrives, *Star Trek* appears poised for a long and prosperous theatrical voyage—and all but guarantees that this crew's five-year mission will continue with a sequel.

Live long and prosper, indeed.

---

*Note: The box office figures above reflect studio weekend estimates; final numbers may vary slightly.*

The Enterprise has landed—and it landed big. Paramount's *Star Trek*, director J.J. Abrams' bold reimagining of the beloved sci-fi saga, dominated the weekend box office with an estimated $76.5 million debut, giving the 43-year-old franchise the biggest opening of its long life.

The reboot, which stars Chris Pine as a young James T. Kirk and Zachary Quinto as Spock, proved that Abrams and Paramount's gamble to attract new fans while honoring the faithful paid off handsomely. Bolstered by strong reviews and an enthusiastic "A" CinemaScore from audiences, the film played beyond the traditional Trekkie base, drawing a broad crowd that skewed—perhaps surprisingly—more mainstream than niche. Add in roughly $4 million from Thursday-night IMAX and preview screenings, and Kirk and company had every reason to celebrate.

The performance marks a triumphant reinvention for a property that had grown creaky at the multiplex; 2002's *Star Trek: Nemesis* limped to a franchise-low finish, prompting Paramount to send the series back to the drawing board. This weekend's numbers suggest the risk was worth it.

Elsewhere in the top five, last week's champ **X-Men Origins: Wolverine** held up respectably in its sophomore frame. While the second-weekend decline was steep, the film's global haul continued to keep 20th Century Fox smiling.

In third place, Fox's family-friendly comedy **Ghosts of Girlfriends Past** proved it had legs, adding an estimated $10.4 million in its second weekend. The Matthew McConaughey–Jennifer Garner romantic riff on Dickens dipped a modest 40 percent, a testament to counter-programming appeal for audiences not in the mood for phasers and photon torpedoes.

Disney's animated import **Earth**, the nature documentary from Disneynature, held on for fourth place with roughly $4.3 million, pushing its running total past $24 million—solid returns for a genre that rarely troubles the top of the chart.

On the specialty front, the weekend's most notable new arrival was **The New Daughter**, though it was Kevin Costner's supernatural thriller that struggled to find footing in limited release. Meanwhile, arthouse holdovers **The Soloist** and **Sunshine Cleaning** continued their modest platform runs as counterprogramming for adult audiences seeking an alternative to the weekend's blockbuster spectacle.

With *Star Trek* leading the charge and the summer season officially heating up, all eyes now turn to next weekend, when Ron Howard's *Angels & Demons*—reuniting Tom Hanks with the Dan Brown universe—looks to challenge the Enterprise's reign. But for now, this galaxy belongs to Kirk, Spock, and a franchise that just proved there's still plenty of life in the final frontier.

2. *X-Men Origins: Wolverine* — $27 million

# Star Trek Boldly Goes to No. 1 with Stellar $72.5 Million Debut

Warp speed, indeed. Paramount's *Star Trek* reboot didn't just meet expectations this weekend—it obliterated them, beaming into theaters with a franchise-record $72.5 million and giving director J.J. Abrams the kind of launch every studio dreams about.

To put that number in perspective: the previous best opening for any *Star Trek* film was *First Contact*'s $30.7 million back in 1996. Abrams' film more than doubled that, proving that a fresh cast, a savvy marketing campaign, and genuine crossover appeal could take this 43-year-old property to places it had never gone before. Strong reviews and an "A" CinemaScore suggest the good word of mouth should keep the Enterprise cruising for weeks to come.

## Wolverine Feels the Sequel Slump

Last weekend's champ, *X-Men Origins: Wolverine*, took the expected sophomore tumble, dropping roughly 69 percent to around $27 million. That's a steep fall, but Hugh Jackman's clawed antihero has still amassed a solid domestic haul north of $130 million. The two comic-book-adjacent blockbusters comfortably split the top two spots, though *Star Trek* clearly won the weekend's battle of the tentpoles.

## The Ladies of Romance and Revenge

The holdovers in the middle of the pack tell an interesting story about counterprogramming.

*Ghosts of Girlfriends Past*, the Matthew McConaughey rom-com, settled into third with about $10.4 million in its second weekend, a modest 41 percent decline that speaks to steady, if unspectacular, interest.

Close behind, *Obsessed*—the Beyoncé-versus-crazed-stalker thriller—continued its respectable run with roughly $6.6 million, pushing its total past the $50 million mark and confirming that its splashy opening was no fluke.

*17 Again*, the Zac Efron body-swap comedy, keeps chugging along in its fourth weekend, adding approximately $4.4 million and demonstrating the kind of leggy staying power that makes modestly budgeted films profitable.

Finally, *Next Day Air*, the Summit Entertainment crime comedy, delivered a decent debut of around $4 million from a limited footprint, a solid per-theater showing that suggests the low-budget effort should turn a tidy profit.

## The Bottom Line

With *Star Trek* leading the charge, the overall box office got a healthy jolt heading into the summer season. The question now is whether Abrams' crew can maintain altitude against the coming wave of blockbusters—but for this weekend, at least, the future of *Star Trek* has rarely looked brighter.

*Check back next week as* Angels & Demons *looks to unlock the top spot.*
